clinical_category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

semantic_correction.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has neutropenia and is being discharged home. Which statement shows correct understanding of infection-prevention teaching?

options.A: I will clean my hands often and call my oncology team immediately if my temperature reaches 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, even after hours.
options.B: If a fever starts overnight, I can wait until the oncology office opens the next morning before reporting it.
options.C: Because my white blood cell count is low, frequent hand hygiene will not meaningfully reduce my infection risk.
options.D: I can observe new infection symptoms for a day or two before calling if they do not interfere with my usual activities.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC states that chemotherapy can reduce infection-fighting white blood cells and cause neutropenia, increasing the risk of serious infection. Current CDC patient guidance instructs people receiving chemotherapy to wash their hands often and to call their clinician immediately for a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. CDC explicitly advises calling right away even in the middle of the night and not waiting until morning because infection during chemotherapy can become life-threatening. CDC also advises prompt reporting of other signs and symptoms of infection. Therefore option A demonstrates correct understanding.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach clients with chemotherapy-related neutropenia to use frequent hand hygiene and immediately report fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher or other infection symptoms.

audit_findings_append.finding: The original answer was uniquely longest and one distractor used absolute wording. The revised item directly tests current CDC neutropenia home-safety teaching with balanced alternatives.

option_audit.A: Correct. It combines CDC-recommended frequent hand hygiene with immediate reporting of fever at 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, including after hours.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. CDC specifically advises not to wait until morning when infection or fever is suspected during chemotherapy.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. CDC recommends frequent hand cleaning because it helps prevent infection during chemotherapy.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. CDC advises calling right away for signs and symptoms of infection rather than waiting for persistence or activity limitation.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone matches both CDC infection-prevention behavior and the required urgency of fever reporting.
cueing_check: All four choices are home-care statements of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
